rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to capture the retention range of all 10 compounds, with ample high-organic hold time for late eluters. The intermediate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in subsequent injections.

Double the gradient slope to shorten retention while testing whether the current resolution margin is sufficient. Keeping starting composition and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient compression.

Test temperature-dependent selectivity at the faster gradient to separate the crowded central peaks without lengthening the run. Raising temperature may also shorten retention, preserving the zero time penalty.

Slightly lengthen the gradient to improve the remaining under-resolved pair while retaining the favorable high-temperature selectivity. The last peak should still elute early enough to avoid a time penalty.

Test whether a slightly shallower gradient and higher temperature provide a larger resolution margin while preserving the maximum CRF. The shallower gradient should help the earlier critical pair, while higher temperature may improve selectivity in the central cluster and offset the added retention.

Return to the successful 55 °C selectivity and modestly reduce the gradient slope relative to injection 4. This tests a nearby method that may preserve CRF 1.000 while improving the earlier critical pair without substantially increasing retention.

Test a higher starting organic fraction at the successful temperature to seek a shorter maximum-score method. This also probes whether shifting the gradient window improves the narrow resolution margin in the central cluster.

Reduce the gradient slope from injection 7 to restore resolution of the earlier critical pair while retaining the higher starting organic fraction. The central pair should remain near baseline resolution, with the last peak still expected inside the zero-penalty time window.

Shift the gradient window upward at the start and reduce its slope to test whether both critical pairs can gain a more balanced resolution margin. Injection 8 already achieves the maximum CRF, so this explores an alternative maximum-score method rather than a higher attainable score.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 8 while retaining its starting composition and temperature. This should improve the earlier critical pair while preserving central-pair resolution and, potentially, the maximum CRF of 1.000.

Probe temperature sensitivity around the maximum-score method from injection 4 by lowering temperature one grid step. This isolates selectivity changes and tests whether full resolution and zero time penalty persist at 50 °C.

Explore low-temperature selectivity with the fast scouting gradient, since nearby changes around 55 °C have yielded only narrow resolution margins. This tests a distinct separation regime for another maximum-score method; CRF 1.000 is already secured.

Test a much faster gradient at high temperature for an alternative selectivity regime, potentially moving the earlier critical pair through an elution-order reversal. This exploratory run seeks a faster maximum-score method, while the established CRF 1.000 methods remain available.

Use a gradient slope between injections 7 and 8, targeting full resolution with a shorter retention time than injection 8. All peaks are expected to elute during the gradient, so the lower final organic fraction should not compromise recovery.

Explore a faster high-temperature alternative by combining a higher starting organic fraction with a gentler slope than injection 13. These changes may rebalance the crowded central peaks; the previously achieved maximum CRF of 1.000 remains the benchmark.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step from injection 15 to test whether the remaining close pair separates further in the reversed-order regime. This seeks a faster maximum-score alternative while monitoring compression of the early peaks.

Build on injection 16 by raising the starting organic fraction to improve its closest pair, while lengthening the gradient to protect separation of the adjacent pair. This tests a faster alternative to the established maximum-score methods, although early-peak resolution may become limiting.

Test a distinct intermediate-temperature selectivity regime at a gradient expected to retain a zero time penalty. The central pair approaches co-elution between 40 and 50 °C under nearby conditions, so this run checks whether an order change produces a useful alternative separation pattern.

Explore the lower-temperature side of the central-pair order reversal, using a longer gradient than the 25 °C scouting run to reduce crowding. This may provide an alternative fully resolved method near the zero-time-penalty boundary.

Return to the successful 55 °C regime and slightly flatten injection 9's gradient to improve its sole under-resolved pair. The central pair has some resolution margin, and the last peak is expected to remain near the zero-time-penalty boundary.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope relative to injection 20 to bring its remaining critical pair above R = 1.5. This tests whether the higher-starting-organic method can also reach CRF 1.000 before a time penalty appears.

Preserve injection 4's successful gradient slope and temperature while ending the gradient earlier at a lower organic fraction. Since its last peak eluted at 7.60 min, before this gradient ends at the outlet at 8.65 min, this method is expected to retain CRF 1.000.

Preserve the successful gradient slope through the crowded peaks, then hold at 50% organic. This tests whether a lower final organic fraction still elutes the isolated last peak within the zero-penalty window and retains CRF 1.000.

Preserve injection 8's starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while ending at 60% organic. Its last peak should elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, reproducing CRF 1.000 and its slightly larger minimum-resolution margin.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 24 to improve the earlier critical pair while retaining adequate central-pair resolution. The last peak is expected near the zero-time-penalty boundary, offering another candidate for the already-achieved maximum CRF of 1.000.
